title: Beating the Sicilian with 3.Bc4 - seriously?
summary:
An underarm serve?

About 20 years ago, developing the bishop to f4 after 1.d4 d5, but without first playing c2-c4, was still mocked. The London System was regarded as an "old man's opening". This disparaging label referred to chess players who, without much knowledge of opening theory, wanted to play a quiet positional game with the white pieces. Many amateurs chose the opening for precisely this reason. Anyone who encountered it with Black in tournament play, however, soon realised that White's setup was not without venom. The London System is now a recognised opening and is practically part of the repertoire of most top players.

The idea of developing the bishop early can just as easily be mirrored on the other side of the board. What is meant here is the move 2...Bc4.

After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6, the development with 3.Bc4 has been known since the beginnings of chess theory. The Italian Game has now even overtaken the Spanish Opening as the most frequently played opening among top professionals after 1.e4 e5, and for good reason: there is neither a Marshall Gambit nor a Berlin Defence in these setups. The move 2.Bc4 has also been known for centuries as the Bishop's Opening.

The situation is quite different with the early development of the bishop to c4 after 1.e4 c5, the Sicilian Defence. This was also played fairly regularly at amateur level. Yet the verdict of opening experts was even more damning than in the case of the London System. A White setup along the lines of 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 (or other second moves for Black) and then 3.Bc4 , 3.d3, 3.0-0, etc., analogous to White's setup in the Modern Variation of the Italian Game, was for a long time not even taken seriously by theoreticians. Even among stronger tournament players, developing the bishop to c4 after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 without first playing d2-d4 was considered unsound, almost like an "underarm serve".

But this assessment too has changed in recent years. On internet chess platforms, most games played by amateurs are played without any particular opening knowledge. Many players are content with using a simple opening setup while playing white, for example: 1.d4, 2.e3, 3.Nf3, 4.Bd3, 5.0-0, more or less regardless of what Black does. The other approach is the Italian setup, i.e. 1.e4, 2.Nf3, 3.Bc4, 4.0-0, 5.d3. Thus, one can play against many of Black's first-move replies without too much difficulty: against 1...e5, 1...d6, 1...g6, 1...Nc6, 1...b6, but also against 1...c5. Against 1...e6 and 1...c6, the Exchange Variation helps. Only against 1...Nf6 and 1...d5 does one need to be careful and come up with something. And just like that, one has a "repertoire".

Kazakhstani tennis star Alexander Bublik has often tried underarm serves even in Grand Slams - here pictured at the 2022 edition of Wimbledon | Image: BBC

In recent years, an incredible number of games, mostly blitz games, have been played on the internet. Grandmasters participate regularly in such events. But the endless repetition of well-known theoretical variations eventually becomes boring. New paths are sought and tested. And so a proliferation of "non-theoretical" or "irregular" opening variations has emerged. The move 3.Bc4 against the Sicilian Defence is one of them.

Among the top players who regularly play 3.Bc4 against the Sicilian, at least in online blitz games, is Magnus Carlsen. If the best player in the world plays it, the move cannot be bad, can it? And if it is good enough for blitz, why not for classical tournament games?

So now more and more top professionals are playing the "amateur move" 3.Bc4 against the Sicilian Defence, including in classical tournament games. One of the latest examples comes from the England v. France match in round six of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand.

Etienne Bacrot playing black against Michael Adams | Photo: Michal Walusza

Michael Adams had no interest in entering a theoretical discussion with Etienne Bacrot in long lines of the Sicilian Defence and, after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6, chose to develop his pieces with 3.Bc4. For a long time, very little happened. But when the game turned interesting, it became clear that White's setup allowed many tactically venomous possibilities.

With the win, Adams was able to offset his teammate Gawain Maroroa Jones' defeat against Marc'Andria Maurizzi. The match ended 2-2.

title: Fagernes: Gloeckler holds outright lead with three rounds to go
summary:
The 14-year-old German prodigy leads Jumabayev by half a point

The Fagernes Autumn Tournament has reached its final stretch, with 14-year-old German IM Christian Gloeckler continuing to lead the GM Swiss. After defeating Austrian IM Lukas Dotzer in Thursday's seventh round, Gloeckler moved to 6/7 and retained sole first place. GM Rinat Jumabayev is his closest pursuer on 5½ points after beating top seed Elham Amar.

The tournament is being played from 3 to 11 October at the Scandic Valdres hotel in Fagernes, around 187 kilometres north of Oslo. The GM group consists of ten rounds spread over nine days, with Tuesday serving as the only double-round day. The format is intended in part to give players greater flexibility when pursuing title norms.

Fagernes, located in the Norwegian Nord-Aurdal Municipality, is the largest urban/commercial centre for the Valdres region | Photo: John Erling Blad via Wikimedia Commons

Gloeckler has held at least a share of the lead since the opening stages. He was the only player to start with 3/3, after the six-way tie that had emerged following round two was broken in the third round.

Tuesday's double round then provided his first encounters with grandmasters: he drew a lengthy game against Jumabayev before defeating third seed Frode Olav Olsen Urkedal later that day. The draw with Jumabayev lasted 84 moves and saw the players agreeing to share the point in an objectively drawn rook endgame in which Gloeckler had an extra pawn.

Christian Gloeckler defeated Frode Olav Olsen Urkedal in round five | Photo: Anniken Vestby

Those results left Gloeckler alone at the top with 4½/5. His sixth-round assignment was another demanding one, as he had black against Amar, the highest-rated player in the field. The Norwegian obtained the more promising position in the endgame, but the advantage gradually disappeared and the game was eventually drawn. Gloeckler therefore entered round seven on 5/6, half a point ahead of a group of challengers.

Dotzer was one of those players, but Gloeckler increased the gap between them in their direct encounter on Thursday. Facing the Austrian's Sicilian Defence, the German employed a familiar attacking plan after the players castled on opposite sides. Gloeckler's kingside offensive eventually decided the game, allowing him to finish the round on 6/7.

An Open Sicilian appears on the board! | Photo: Anniken Vestby

The victory continued Gloeckler's strong run against titled opposition. His performance is relevant to his pursuit of another grandmaster norm. The youngster earned his first GM norm earlier this year at the Biel Chess Festival, where he scored 8/9 in the Master Open and recorded a performance rating of 2688.

Jumabayev was the only member of the chasing group to win in round seven. The Kazakh grandmaster defeated Amar to reach 5½/7 and is now alone in second place, half a point behind Gloeckler. Their earlier meeting means that the two leading players will not face each other again during the remaining three rounds.

Gloeckler thus enters that closing stage with the outright lead he has maintained since the middle of the tournament. The tenth and final round will be played on Sunday 11 October.

Rinat Jumabayev playing 2.c4 against Elham Amar | Photo: Anniken Vestby

Indian rising star Sarbartho Mani, aged 10, has collected 4/7 points so far in Fagernes - he comes from obtaining a 4/9 score in Group B of the Legends & Prodigies Tournament in Madrid! | Photo: Anniken Vestby
